question: A webhook receiver pushes every incoming event into a module-level array and a worker loop takes them out with `events.shift()`. Under a traffic spike the process slows down and later crashes. Which two problems does the design have?
options: `push` is O(n) and arrays cannot hold more than 65 536 items
`shift` is O(n) per dequeue, and the queue is unbounded, so memory grows until the process dies
Arrays are not thread safe in Node.js
The worker loop should use `pop` to make it faster
explanation: Use a head index (or ring buffer) for O(1) dequeues and a maximum size with a policy for when it is full. `pop` would make it LIFO and process the newest events first.

question: A signup creates a user, then a workspace, then charges a card. The charge fails. In which order should the compensations run?
options: Delete the user, then delete the workspace
Refund the charge, delete the workspace, delete the user
Delete the workspace, then delete the user
No compensation: a database transaction covers the card provider too
explanation: Undo only what completed, newest first: the workspace depends on the user. The charge never succeeded, so there is nothing to refund, and external APIs are not covered by your database transaction.

question: Order confirmation emails are queued in an in-memory queue inside the API process. What happens on a deploy?
options: The queued emails are lost when the old process stops; use a durable queue (Redis/BullMQ, pg-boss, SQS) for work users depend on
Node.js persists module variables between restarts
The new process receives the queue automatically
Nothing, because emails are sent synchronously
explanation: In-memory structures die with the process. Durable queues keep jobs across restarts, share them between instances and add retries.
